Callers that used EXEC sales.refresh_daily; are updated to CALL SALES.REFRESH_DAILY();
explanations: Snowflake has no macros, so the Teradata macro becomes a Snowflake Scripting stored procedure. Call it with CALL SALES.REFRESH_DAILY() or CALL SALES.REFRESH_DAILY('2025-01-01'::DATE) instead of EXEC.
The default argument value is kept: P_DAY DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE(), so an omitted argument means today's date, as in Teradata.
The single INSERT ... SELECT is kept unchanged except for :P_DAY variable binding and naming-map identifiers (SALES."ACCOUNT", SALES.DAILY_BALANCE).
EXECUTE AS OWNER is declared explicitly (rule snowflake.rule.procedure_execute_as) and mirrors Teradata macro owner-rights execution.
The procedure contains no DDL and no explicit transaction. The single INSERT is atomic under autocommit, matching the macro's single-request transaction.

-- Converted: Teradata CREATE MACRO sales.refresh_daily(p_day DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE) -> Snowflake Scripting stored procedure SALES.REFRESH_DAILY with an optional DATE argument that defaults to CURRENT_DATE(), LANGUAGE SQL, EXECUTE AS OWNER, returning the number of rows inserted.
-- Reason: Snowflake has no macros; procedural logic is ported to Snowflake Scripting procedures. Every procedure must declare EXECUTE AS; OWNER matches Teradata macro semantics, where the macro runs with its owning database's privileges and the caller needs only EXEC on the macro.
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE SALES.REFRESH_DAILY(P_DAY DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE())
  RETURNS NUMBER
  LANGUAGE SQL
  EXECUTE AS OWNER
AS
$$
BEGIN
  -- Converted: INSERT ... SELECT p_day, account_id, balance FROM sales.account -> same INSERT ... SELECT, with the parameter bound as :P_DAY and the reserved table name quoted as SALES."ACCOUNT".
  -- Reason: Snowflake Scripting references variables in SQL statements with a colon prefix. ACCOUNT is a reserved word in Snowflake, so the naming map gives the table as SALES."ACCOUNT".
  INSERT INTO SALES.DAILY_BALANCE (BALANCE_DATE, ACCOUNT_ID, AMOUNT)
  SELECT :P_DAY, ACCOUNT_ID, BALANCE
  FROM SALES."ACCOUNT";

  -- Converted: The implicit Teradata macro activity count -> RETURN SQLROWCOUNT.
  -- Reason: Callers keep the inserted-row count that Teradata reports as ACTIVITY_COUNT after EXEC.
  RETURN SQLROWCOUNT;
END;
$$;

-- Converted: CREATE VIEW sales.customer_accounts -> CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW SALES.CUSTOMER_ACCOUNTS COPY GRANTS; sales.account -> SALES."ACCOUNT" (quoted), and the implicit JOIN is written as INNER JOIN with AS aliases.
-- Reason: ACCOUNT is a reserved word in Snowflake, so the naming map gives it as a quoted uppercase identifier. OR REPLACE makes redeployment repeatable, and COPY GRANTS keeps grants already on the view when it is replaced.
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW SALES.CUSTOMER_ACCOUNTS
  COPY GRANTS
AS
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.customer_name,
  a.account_id,
  a.balance
FROM SALES.CUSTOMER AS c
INNER JOIN SALES."ACCOUNT" AS a
  ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id;

-- Converted: CREATE VIEW sales.customer_external_rate -> CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW SALES.CUSTOMER_EXTERNAL_RATE COPY GRANTS; Names now follow the naming map. The ANSI DATE '2025-01-01' literal, which Snowflake supports natively, is kept. The non-correlated join predicate is kept as written.
-- Reason: The ON clause filters EXTERNAL_RATE to one date and does not relate the two tables, so the result is every customer paired with every rate row for that date. Keeping the predicate exactly as written preserves this cross-product behavior. OR REPLACE makes redeployment repeatable, and COPY GRANTS keeps grants already on the view when it is replaced.
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW SALES.CUSTOMER_EXTERNAL_RATE
  COPY GRANTS
AS
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  e.rate
FROM SALES.CUSTOMER AS c
INNER JOIN SALES.EXTERNAL_RATE AS e
  ON e.rate_date = DATE '2025-01-01';
